chunk_findings.detail: Decision 1 promises that "the default template for each kind reproduces today's ids exactly", and Decision 2 calls the token set "the full set" — but the token set `{prefix} {seq} {date} {slug} {hash} {parent} {phase} {env} {user-text}` has no token for the pid, while the Context explicitly lists `services/sessions.new_session_id` as an id minted today with shape `s<UTC timestamp>-<pid>`. The session default therefore cannot be expressed with the listed tokens, so the "sees no change / replay byte-identically" guarantee is false for sessions. Worse, the validation rule ("a template that could produce the same id twice without `{seq}` or `{hash}` refused") would reject the session default outright, because `s{date}-…` contains neither `{seq}` nor `{hash}`; a project that "sets nothing" and inherits the documented default would fail validation. Either the token set must gain the missing token, or the default/validation claims must be narrowed.

chunk_findings.detail: Decision 3 says that on an offline clash "the record that is later in the fold order keeps its id unchanged and gains the alias `<id>.<clone suffix>` … Nothing is renumbered." Since aliases are additive (Decision 4: ids are never renamed), the earlier colliding record also retains the id `BUG-123`. Two records therefore end up with the same canonical id `BUG-123`, and the disambiguating alias `BUG-123.b` is attached to the other (winning) record, not the loser: a lookup of `BUG-123` still resolves to two records, and a lookup of `BUG-123.b` returns the record that already had the plain id, i.e. the alias cannot be used to reach the losing record. This contradicts the stated goal that a clash "produces a visible suffix, not a silent duplicate." Concretely, two clones minting `BUG-123` offline and then merging leave an ambiguous `BUG-123`, which `show`/doctor cannot resolve. Either the losing record's canonical lookup key must become the suffixed name (a rename, which Decision 4 forbids) or the alias must be attached to the losing record, and the doc does not say how the two same-id records are told apart.

chunk_findings.detail: The rule now declares a template valid if it contains "at least one source of uniqueness: `{seq}`, `{hash}`, `{digest}` (deliberately stable), or `{time}` together with `{pid}`." But the preceding sentence in the same item defines `{digest}` as a deterministic content digest whose whole point is that "the same failing check maps to the same bug," i.e. filing the same text twice yields ONE id, not two. So the example template `Bci-{slug}-{digest}` — which the text itself presents as a shipped default — satisfies the "uniqueness" requirement while doing exactly what the original rule forbade ("a template that could produce the same id twice without `{seq}` or `{hash}` refused"). Listing `{digest}` among the uniqueness sources makes the validation rule self-contradictory: a template consisting only of `{digest}` (plus `{slug}`/`{prefix}`) is accepted, yet it can mint a duplicate key for identical content. Either `{digest}` must not count as a uniqueness source, or it needs an explicit, separate carve-out for the deliberately-stable CI-bug case.

chunk_findings.detail:
The rewritten validation rule accepts any template that "must declare `stable = true`" when it lacks `{seq}`, `{hash}`, or `{time}`+`{pid}`, but it never requires a stable template to actually contain a content-determined token (`{digest}`). It only imposes the converse ("`{digest}` is allowed only in stable templates"). Two concrete cases fall through:

1. Volatile token in a "stable" template: config `template = "{prefix}-{date}"` (or `"{prefix}-{time}"`, `"{prefix}-{pid}"`) has no listed uniqueness source, so it satisfies the rule by declaring `stable = true`. Yet `{date}`/`{time}`/`{pid}` change between filings, so filing identical content the next day produces a different id. This directly contradicts the next sentence, "A stable template maps the same content to the same id on purpose, so filing it again extends the existing record instead of creating a new one." The pre-change rule refused this template; the change now admits it.

2. Colliding "stable" template: config `template = "B{slug}"` with `stable = true` is admitted, and two different reports that happen to share a slug map to the same id, silently extending an unrelated record. Since the rule does not require `{digest}` (or any deterministic content token) in stable templates, the stated guarantee ("maps the same content to the same id") is not enforced in either direction.

A correct rule would require stable templates to contain `{digest}` and to exclude volatile tokens (`{date}`, `{time}`, `{pid}`, `{env}`, `{hash}`), e.g. `Bci-{slug}-{digest}`. As written, a config that passes validation can violate the semantic the paragraph claims for it.

chunk_findings.detail: The clash rule silently renames a user-visible id, contradicting both the same paragraph ("No event changes, and nothing is renumbered or renamed") and decision 4 ("A recorded id is never renamed"). The key is explicitly defined as "the record's KEY, which is what people see and type and what ddflow prints"; the later record's key being "shown as `BUG-123.<clone suffix>`" is therefore a rename, not an alias. Concrete scenario: clone A and clone B both work offline and each file a bug, so both mint key `BUG-123`. B's users type `BUG-123` into a commit message. After the logs meet, B's record is reassigned the key `BUG-123.b`, and the string `BUG-123` in B's commit now resolves to A's record. The doc's own remedy for disagreements is "aliases only" (decision 4), but no alias is used; the loser's printed id is changed. The statement that nothing is renamed is false.
chunk_findings.title: docs/ddflow/decisions/id-schemes.md — section 3 "Sequential numbers" (clash handling)

chunk_findings.detail: The rule accepts `{time}`+`{pid}` as "a source of uniqueness," but `{time}` is defined two bullets earlier as "UTC timestamp, second resolution." Two records minted by the same process within one calendar second therefore produce identical keys, so the rule does not guarantee uniqueness. Concrete input: a project sets `[ids] task = "T-{time}-{pid}"`; the validation accepts it as unique; a script then creates two tasks in the same second from the same process, and both get key `T-20261005120000-4242`. This also undercuts the claim "All agents on one machine share the log, so a key is unique there" and "Each shipped default passes these rules" (the session default `s{time}-{pid}` has exactly this collision window).

chunk_findings.detail: The new sentences say the id service "checks every key it mints against every id and key of every kind in the folded log ... A key that is already taken gets `-2`, `-3`, and so on." Two sentences later the doc keeps: "A stable template maps the same content to the same id on purpose, so filing it again extends the existing record instead of creating a new one." These two rules give contradictory outcomes for the *same* condition ("the key I just computed is already in the log"): the new rule says mint a new, suffixed key (`…-2`), the stable rule says reuse/extend the existing record. Concrete input: a stable template such as `note-{slug}` with `stable = true`; file it once (record gets key `note-foo`), then file identical content again. The second filing computes `note-foo`, the check finds it "already taken", and the new rule produces a second record whose key is `note-foo-2` instead of extending the first — breaking the idempotency the stable paragraph promises. Unless the check is explicitly carved out for stable templates (the diff does not say so, and it says "every key it mints"), the two adjacent rules conflict and the doc no longer tells an implementer which branch wins.

chunk_findings.detail: The clash rule silently renames a user-visible id, contradicting both the same paragraph ("No event changes, and nothing is renumbered or renamed") and decision 4 ("A recorded id is never renamed"). The key is explicitly defined as "the record's KEY, which is what people see and type and what ddflow prints"; the later record's key being "shown as `BUG-123.<clone suffix>`" is therefore a rename, not an alias. Concrete scenario: clone A and clone B both work offline and each file a bug, so both mint key `BUG-123`. B's users type `BUG-123` into a commit message. After the logs meet, B's record is reassigned the key `BUG-123.b`, and the string `BUG-123` in B's commit now resolves to A's record. The doc's own remedy for disagreements is "aliases only" (decision 4), but no alias is used; the loser's printed id is changed. The statement that nothing is renamed is false.

chunk_findings.detail: The rule accepts `{time}`+`{pid}` as "a source of uniqueness," but `{time}` is defined two bullets earlier as "UTC timestamp, second resolution." Two records minted by the same process within one calendar second therefore produce identical keys, so the rule does not guarantee uniqueness. Concrete input: a project sets `[ids] task = "T-{time}-{pid}"`; the validation accepts it as unique; a script then creates two tasks in the same second from the same process, and both get key `T-20261005120000-4242`. This also undercuts the claim "All agents on one machine share the log, so a key is unique there" and "Each shipped default passes these rules" (the session default `s{time}-{pid}` has exactly this collision window).

chunk_findings.detail: `{seq}` is allocated "for that kind" (per-kind counter), and the validation rule only requires that the template contain one of `{seq}`, `{hash}`, or `{time}`+`{pid}`; nothing requires a token that distinguishes kinds. So the validation admits configs where two different kinds mint the same key. Concrete input: `[ids] task = "{seq}"` and `[ids] bug = "{seq}"`; the first task and first bug both get key `1`. The doc nevertheless asserts that a key "is unique there" and that a key can be resolved to the internal id before recording; with a non-unique key, `ddflow show 1` (accepting a bare key) resolves to two records, so the resolution contract cannot hold. The validation that is supposed to make every template legal does not prevent this.

chunk_findings.detail: The new sentences say the id service "checks every key it mints against every id and key of every kind in the folded log ... A key that is already taken gets `-2`, `-3`, and so on." Two sentences later the doc keeps: "A stable template maps the same content to the same id on purpose, so filing it again extends the existing record instead of creating a new one." These two rules give contradictory outcomes for the *same* condition ("the key I just computed is already in the log"): the new rule says mint a new, suffixed key (`…-2`), the stable rule says reuse/extend the existing record. Concrete input: a stable template such as `note-{slug}` with `stable = true`; file it once (record gets key `note-foo`), then file identical content again. The second filing computes `note-foo`, the check finds it "already taken", and the new rule produces a second record whose key is `note-foo-2` instead of extending the first — breaking the idempotency the stable paragraph promises. Unless the check is explicitly carved out for stable templates (the diff does not say so, and it says "every key it mints"), the two adjacent rules conflict and the doc no longer tells an implementer which branch wins.

chunk_findings.detail: `{hash}` is defined as "the salted hash of `auto_id`", but Decision 1 requires the default template for each kind to reproduce today's ids byte-identically, and the auto id is `{prefix}` + ten hex digits of the salted hash of the *text* (e.g. `B9c56de9d58`). If `{hash}` really hashes `auto_id` (which already contains those ten hex digits), the default template `{prefix}{hash}` renders `B` + `salted_hash("B9c56de9d58")`, not `B9c56de9d58`. That breaks the two central promises of the change ("the default template for each kind reproduces today's ids exactly" and "existing logs replay byte-identically"). Either `{hash}` must be defined as the hash *body* of `auto_id` (the ten hex digits themselves, salted from the text), or the auto-id default cannot be written as a template. As written, a conforming implementation of the default produces different ids.

chunk_findings.detail: The uniqueness rule states the id service checks a minted key "against every id and key of every kind in the folded log", and that "keys share one namespace across kinds", while §4 says any record "may carry aliases … accepted everywhere an id is accepted" and Consequences says keys are "the same mechanism as aliases". Aliases are therefore part of the same resolution space, but the mint-time collision check enumerates only ids and keys — not aliases — and there is no rule anywhere for a key colliding with an alias. Concrete input: an existing record R carries the project label/alias `BUG-123` (exactly the JIRA-style form the doc is trying to enable); later, a kind with template `BUG-{seq}` reaches seq 123 and mints key `BUG-123`, because no id-or-key collision exists. Now `show BUG-123` matches two candidates (R via alias, the new record via key), and unlike the cross-clone key ambiguity — which is explicitly defined to refuse with exit 3 and list candidates — there is no defined outcome here. The check must include aliases, or aliases must be excluded from the key namespace, otherwise the "no silent ambiguous reference" guarantee is not met.

chunk_findings.detail:
The change puts aliases into the same "taken key" namespace that §3's stable-template exception operates on, and the two rules then disagree about what a collision means. §3 (as amended) says the service "checks every key it mints against every id, key **and alias**," and the very next sentence says that when a key "is already taken" the filing "extends that record." §4, however, says a minted key that collides with an alias "gets a suffix, like any taken key." For a stable template these are mutually exclusive outcomes, and neither section scopes the exception to id/key collisions only.

Concrete failure: record R has id `Bfoo`; later a stable template `{prefix}{slug}` is used for a check whose slug is `foo`, giving key `Bfoo`. Filing that check is supposed to be idempotent (the "taken key IS the expected match" case). Now suppose a different record R2 carries the alias `Bfoo` (permitted, since at add time `Bfoo` was not yet any id/key/alias, or the alias arrived via a clone merge, which §4 explicitly allows). The mint now sees `Bfoo` as "taken" — by R2's alias — and §3 tells it to treat that as a match and "extend that record," i.e. extend R2, which is not the stable template's record. If instead §4 is followed, it mints `Bfoo-2`, silently breaking the stable template's idempotency (the next filing mints `Bfoo-3`, and so on). The decision doc records no rule resolving this, so implementers will apply the stable-template branch first (it is stated as the exception) and corrupt the wrong record, or apply the alias branch and make stable templates non-stable. Either reading is wrong for the same input; §4 needs to carve the stable-template case out of "any taken key," or §3 needs to state that the expected match applies only to collisions with an existing *id/key* of the same template, never with an alias.

data.decision: Operator answers 2026-10-05 (next-free sequence with suffix on clash; full token set; aliases only; vocabulary also as CLI/MCP names), made precise by review: (1) [ids] template per kind, defaults reproduce today's ids exactly ({prefix}{hash} = auto_id's salted blake2b hex; sessions s{time}-{pid}; CI bugs Bci-{slug}-{digest} stable). (2) Tokens {prefix} {seq} {date} {slug} {hash} {parent} {phase} {env} {user-text} plus {time} {pid} {digest}; a template needs {seq}, {hash} or {time}+{pid}, else stable=true, which requires {digest} and only content/kind-fixed tokens. (3) Every record keeps an internal id (minted as today) that events use; {seq} templates produce a KEY resolved to it. Ids, keys and aliases share one namespace; the id service checks each minted key against all of them under the log lock and suffixes a taken key -2, -3; a stable template extends only a same-kind key match and refuses any other collision. (4) Offline clone clash: recorded keys unchanged; the bare key becomes ambiguous (refused, exit 3, candidates listed); both printed with clone suffixes; doctor lists ambiguous free-text references. Caller-named ids keep the CONTESTED/resolve flow. (5) Recorded ids never renamed; aliases on any record; alias adds refused when the name is taken; no bulk migration. (6) [vocabulary] words in human text and as aliases for CLI commands and MCP tools (calls by alias always accepted; advertised only when the tier allows); event kinds, JSON keys and canonical tool names unchanged. Full text: docs/ddflow/decisions/id-schemes.md.

data.summary: core/flowsignals.reviewer_latency_ratio takes the median of (review gate outcome ts - gate.started ts) over 30 min, divided by a 7-day median. That interval includes the agent's triage and fixes between rounds, gates recorded by hand after triage, and diff size (delta reviews of 560-695k chars after merging main). It does not measure how long the reviewer took to answer. Observed 2026-10-06: 'parallel: 2 (auto: ceiling 8; limited by reviewer latency ratio)' while the deepseek vLLM server reported 3 running, 0 waiting and 0.1% KV cache, i.e. nearly idle. Fix: measure reviewer service time per chunk (the durations ddflow review already records per chunk), normalised by chunk size, and treat it as saturation only when it rises while the reviewer's in-flight count is high; where the server exposes queue metrics (vLLM /metrics num_requests_waiting), prefer them. Regression test: long triage gaps and large diffs at constant per-chunk service time must not raise the ratio.
data.title: reviewer_latency_ratio measures wall time from gate.started to the gate outcome, not reviewer service time: an idle reviewer server shrinks parallelism

data.summary: Reported by U3 on 2026-10-06. After 'git merge main' into an item branch, 'ddflow review <id> --delta' diffs from the last reviewed head to HEAD. That range includes every commit that came in from main, so the reviewer gets 560-695k characters of other items' code, already reviewed elsewhere, instead of the item's own change. It wastes reviewer capacity, inflates review latency and produces findings about other agents' code (refuted by hand). Agents worked around it with --commit. Fix: the delta should be (merge-base(HEAD, main) .. HEAD) minus what was already reviewed, i.e. exclude commits reachable from main (git diff with --first-parent or a range diff against main's merged commits). Regression test: review, merge main with unrelated changes, delta-review: only the item's own new changes are sent.

data.question: What must change architecturally so ddflow upgrades smoothly, minor or major (like P-unify), across event log, derived stores, config, CLI/MCP/JSON interfaces and the artifacts adopted into user projects, including mixed-version clones?

data.decision: Operator 2026-10-06. (1) Every renamed or removed CLI command, flag, MCP tool, tool argument and config key keeps working through a declared alias with a one-line deprecation notice until ddflow 1.0 (hidden from help and tools/list, never removed before 1.0); ddflow upgrade rewrites ddflow-managed references to the new names; releases are versioned by impact (a declared breaking change is a minor bump while 0.x), not patch-bumped automatically. (2) An older ddflow meeting data written by a newer one writes what it understands and preserves everything it does not understand untouched (unknown keys, sections, fields, regions, event kinds); it is refused (exit 3, 'upgrade ddflow to >= X') only on a DIRECT CONFLICT: a write that would lose, overwrite or downgrade content a newer version wrote (e.g. re-rendering a managed file stamped by a newer ddflow, rewriting a config section in a newer format, minting ids under a scheme it cannot apply). (3) B-upgrade.2 manifest, .3 plan, .4 apply, .5 repairs, .6 notice and .7 end-to-end test are part of P-unify's finish line; .8-.11 stay after it. Research R-compat.
